title: Anchor — Productivity System for J.C. Liechty
claims: Anchor is a single-folder personal productivity and R&D command system built for J.C. Liechty, running as a persistent local web server (the `anchor` Windows service on http://localhost:8777) that reads and writes plain-markdown task, project, and inbox files directly — no database, Python stdlib only. Beyond ordinary task management (dashboard, domains, cancel/save/restore lifecycles, a 5 AM self-test health check), its heart is an R&D "Mission Control" surface that launches a research → planning → build agent trio (researchPrime → Crucible → Foreman) as durable, worktree-isolated Claude/Gemini terminal sessions, then persists, summarizes, links, and organizes the documents each effort produces. The system has matured through many shipped waves (v2 through v12, plus Gandalf deep-think reviews and a telemetry/resume overhaul), so the core is deployed and heavily exercised in daily use. Current active work centers on durability and safety: a "safe-to-arm" freeze-only zombie-session reaper being brought to a numeric, John-flips-it-on gate, alongside a Skill Foundry v2 build and a queued log-structured storage rearchitecture. Recent lane activity shows planning and build handoffs plus deliverables like the Foreman and Foundry execution logs, reflecting a project that is production-live for its owner but not yet hardened for sharing with outside collaborators.

Anchor is a personal productivity and R&D command system built for J.C. Liechty, running as a persistent local web server (a Windows service on http://localhost:8777) that reads and writes plain markdown files with no database and essentially no external dependencies. Its core job is twofold: a daily task/project dashboard (capture, prioritize, complete, cancel, or defer tasks across academic, commercial, family, and writing domains) and a "Mission Control" surface for driving an AI build trio — research (researchPrime), planning (Crucible), and build (Foreman) — as durable, resumable, worktree-isolated terminal sessions with linked handoffs, per-project summaries, cost rollups, and a searchable Boneyard for discarded work. The system is mature and heavily iterated, having shipped through roughly a dozen feature waves (v2 through v12) plus a Gandalf deep-review tab and a model-flexible execution layer that honestly degrades when only one AI engine is available. Current active work centers on durability and honesty hardening — including a "safe-to-arm" freeze-only zombie-session reaper whose concrete end state is a reversible freeze that John can finally "flip on" behind a numeric arm gate — alongside recent execution logs for Anchor's own durability waves and the Skill Foundry v2 build. A recent comprehensive review rated it class-leading and honestly engineered for its niche but flagged that it is not yet safely shareable due to open-by-default security gaps, so distribution remains a known open item.

# Anchor — Productivity System for J.C. Liechty

*Project summary · validated, cached*

## Objective

Anchor is a single-folder personal productivity and R&D command system built for J.C. Liechty, running as a persistent local web server (the `anchor` Windows service on http://localhost:8777) that reads and writes plain-markdown task, project, and inbox files directly — no database, Python stdlib only. Beyond ordinary task management (dashboard, domains, cancel/save/restore lifecycles, a 5 AM self-test health check), its heart is an R&D "Mission Control" surface that launches a research → planning → build agent trio (researchPrime → Crucible → Foreman) as durable, worktree-isolated Claude/Gemini terminal sessions, then persists, summarizes, links, and organizes the documents each effort produces. The system has matured through many shipped waves (v2 through v12, plus Gandalf deep-think reviews and a telemetry/resume overhaul), so the core is deployed and heavily exercised in daily use. Current active work centers on durability and safety: a "safe-to-arm" freeze-only zombie-session reaper being brought to a numeric, John-flips-it-on gate, alongside a Skill Foundry v2 build and a queued log-structured storage rearchitecture. Recent lane activity shows planning and build handoffs plus deliverables like the Foreman and Foundry execution logs, reflecting a project that is production-live for its owner but not yet hardened for sharing with outside collaborators.
